newsitem.title: USA: Stocks, bonds rally as data dispels rate hike fears.
newsitem.headline: Stocks, bonds rally as data dispels rate hike fears.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks soared into record territory and bonds rallied on Friday as Wall Street cheered the government's May employment report for being weak enough to ward off an interest rate hike by the Federal Reserve.
The dollar fell in reaction to the same report, and on talk of a delay in Europe's planned single currency, which strengthened the German mark.
Platinum and palladium prices stayed high, with little sign that market tensions would ease in the near future.

At 1:45 p.m. EDT (1745 GMT), the Dow Jones industrial average was up 106.02 points, or 1.45 percent, at 7,411.31, after rising as high as 7,427.19 earlier. The blue-chip index's record close was 7,383.41 set on May 27.
In the broader market, advancing issues outpaced declines by a 15-7 margin on volume of 261 million shares on the NYSE. The Nasdaq composite index rose 7.09 points to 1,397.14.
Stocks rose along with bonds. The 30-year Treasury rose nearly one point, lowering its yield to 6.80 percent from 6.88 percent at Thursday's close. Prices and yields move in opposite directions.

"The market has decided the unemployment number could have been much worse," said Pierre Ellis, senior economist at Primark Decision Economics. "If the employment report had been strong across the board, the Fed would have appeared likely to tighten. Now it is confusing."

The Labour Department said 138,000 new jobs were created in May, lower than economists had expected and down from a revised 323,000 in April. The unemployment rate fell to 4.8 percent in May from 4.9 percent in April.
Market watchers said the data pointed to both an economic slowdown and a tighter labour market, which could make any interest rate increase harder to justify.

Fed policy-makers held short-term rates steady last month after raising them a quarter point in March, the first increase in more than two years, in a bid to ward off inflation. They meet again early next month to weigh their next move on rates.

"The market needed to see slower employment growth, and it lucked out," said Robert Froehlich, chief investment strategist at Kemper Funds. "This heightens the political pressure on the Federal Reserve not to raise rates."
The stock market was also gleeful because it believed the closely watched jobs report was its last major hurdle before the Fed's July meeting, analysts said.
"Numbers coming before the July meeting, like retail sales and inflation, don't look too powerful," Ellis said. "Some usual things which could go wrong don't look like they will."
Nearly all sectors took part in the rally, with interest-rate-sensitive financial and bank stocks surging, along with some high-technology shares, smaller stocks and energy and transport issues.
In currency trading, the dollar fell to 1.7275 German marks late in New York from 1.7290 marks late on Thursday, and slid to 114.23 Japanese yen from 115.72 yen late Thursday.

"The reason the dollar has sold off is that there are rumours in the market that there will be an announcement of a delay in EMU," said Richard Vullo, vice president at Bayerische Hypotheken und Wechselbank in New York. EMU, or European Monetary Union, refers to the single currency plan.

In commodities, spot platinum stood at about $482.75 an ounce after rising earlier to $500, the highest since 1990. Spot palladium was indicated at $225 an ounce, after touching a 17-year high earlier this week.

Overseas, London's FTSE 100 index jumped 68.8 points, or 1.5 percent, to 4,645.0, for a gain of 23.7 from last Friday. In Tokyo, the 225-share Nikkei average fell 2.40 points to 20,485.75, but was up 416.94 for the week.
